classification.difficultyReason: Requires comparison of radical and polynomial graphs, rejection of inadmissible squared roots, and preservation of an isolated equality point. Higher-degree inequality analysis is the closest available catalogue match.

inlines.text: The graphs meet at (2, 2); for x > 0, the parabola is on or above the radical graph from x = 2 onwards.

answer.worked:
For $x>0$, the two graphs are increasing inverse branches, so their intersection lies on $y=x$.
$$\begin{align*}x^2-2&=x\\x^2-x-2&=0\\(x-2)(x+1)&=0\end{align*}$$
The condition $x>0$ leaves the intersection $(2,2)$. The sketch shows $y=x^2-2$ on or above $y=\sqrt{x+2}$ when $x\ge2$.

spec.mathematics: The increasing inverse branches meet at (2,2). The parabola is above the radical graph for x>2. Blue identifies the parabola; orange identifies the radical graph.

inlines.text: Compare the two graphs on their common domain, retaining the isolated equality at x = −1.

answer.worked:
The radical requires $x\ge-1$. Equality also requires $x^2-1\ge0$, so an intersection can occur only at $x=-1$ or $x\ge1$.
$$\begin{align*}x^2-1&=\sqrt{x+1}\\(x^2-1)^2&=x+1\\x^4-2x^2-x&=0\\x(x+1)(x^2-x-1)&=0\end{align*}$$
The candidates $x=0$ and $x=\frac{1-\sqrt5}{2}$ fail the original equality. The intersections occur at $x=-1$ and $x=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$. The sketch shows the parabola on or above the radical graph only at the isolated point $x=-1$ and for
$$x\ge\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}.$$
Thus $x=-1$ or $x\ge\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$.

spec.description: Graphs on the common domain x≥−1, with the isolated endpoint intersection and positive intersection marked.
spec.mathematics: Intersections are (-1,0) and (φ,φ), where φ=(1+√5)/2. Between them the parabola is below the radical graph; after φ it is above. The condition x>0 from part (a) is not applied.
